title: The repeated experiences of Graduations, Technology and Playgrounds.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton ties three recent reads to his central claim that whatever children repeatedly experience is what becomes sticky in their brains. A writer worrying about ever-multiplying kindergarten graduations prompts the question of what children learn when ordinary accomplishments are publicly celebrated. Jared Cooney's testimony linking falling test results since 2020 to technology leads Skelton to ask whether children are making sticky the idea that they must adapt to devices rather than the reverse. A Big Think essay on the invention of the playground suggests that sanitised, supervised childhood narrowed choice and decision making. He concedes the technology data could reflect a mismatch between old tests and new priorities, then closes with three reflective questions for learning-focused schools about the kinds of people they are developing and the experiences they repeat.
points: What children, colleagues and parents repeatedly experience determines what becomes sticky, whether or not adults intended it.
Cooney's claim that tech-driven reading habits train skimming rather than thoughtful attention is presented as a repeated-experience problem, with Skelton noting a possible test mismatch caveat.
Playgrounds, graduations and super-involved parenting are read as examples of adult mimicry replacing age-appropriate childhood experience.
Schools are urged to audit the experiences they repeat for students, parents and colleagues, not just the content they teach.
quotes: I have put ‘little by little’ in bold because that’s what repeated experiences look like. The small repeated events that, little by little, get recognised by the brain as worth making sticky.
Do we want children to learn that everything they do has to be celebrated publicly by others? (Just think of the consequences of that.)

Cooney says that this decline correlates with the introduction of more technology into schools. He argues that the breadth of evidence suggests not just correlation but causation. He says that the repeated experience of technology of all kinds - phones, computers, iPads - that occurs anywhere - schools, homes and more - and which are official or unofficial, is profound.

Once upon a time we knew what we wanted our kids to be able to do and created experiences that (for better and worse) enabled that to happen. Now, we are asking our kids to adapt to the technology that is ever more available and ever more sexy with too little thought to the consequences.
Childhood increasingly no longer seems like an age-appropriate expression of different developmental stages on the way to adulthood. Now, it seems more like an age-inappropriate mimicry of it.
And, lets say it. It’s the repeated experiences we have chosen to give our children and students that determine what becomes sticky or not.

It’s our job in learning-focused schools to think about what our children and students are learning as a result of the repeated experiences we provide for them. The repeated experiences should be those which help children and young people develop in ways we think matter.
